findings.title: limitFunction drops every caller argument before invoking the wrapped function
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is declared without rest parameters and always calls function_() with no arguments: `return () => limit(() => function_());`.
findings.impact: Any consumer using the documented and typed `limitFunction(fn, options)` helper with a parameterized function gets undefined arguments at runtime. This silently corrupts inputs while TypeScript promises the returned function accepts and forwards the original argument list.
findings.evidence: index.js:121-125 drops arguments; index.d.ts:133-136 declares `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`; readme.md:126 shows the returned function being passed directly to Array.from, which relies on forwarded callback arguments.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module: `const limited = limitFunction(async value => value, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited('kept?'));` printed `undefined`.

findings.title: limit.map omits the mapper index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The implementation gates index forwarding on `Array.isArray(iterable)` and passes `undefined` for Sets, iterators, and other iterables.
findings.impact: The public API says every mapper receives `(value, index)` and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`, but non-array iterable consumers receive undefined indexes. Batch processors that use indexes for ordering, labels, offsets, or IDs behave differently depending only on iterable type.
findings.evidence: index.js:107-113 passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`; index.d.ts:30-42 and readme.md:78-85 document an index for iterable inputs; tests cover Set/iterator values but do not assert the index argument.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module: `await pLimit(1).map(new Set(['a', 'b']), async (value, index) => seen.push([value, index]));` produced undefined indexes.

findings.title: Options-object construction flips rejectOnClear default from false to true
findings.cause: The options destructuring uses `rejectOnClear = true` even though the variable was initialized to false and the public docs declare a false default.
findings.impact: Calling `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` changes clearQueue semantics from discarding queued work while leaving returned promises pending to actively rejecting all pending promises with AbortError. Users adopting the options object for concurrency alone can get unexpected Promise.all rejection paths.
findings.evidence: index.js:4 initializes `rejectOnClear` to false, but index.js:6-8 overwrites the missing option with true; readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 state `Default: false`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module: with `const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1});` and one running plus one pending task, `limit.clearQueue()` made the pending promise win a race as `rejected:AbortError`.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass runtime validation
findings.cause: The validation checks `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so only truthy non-booleans are rejected.
findings.impact: Invalid JavaScript callers can pass `0`, empty string, or `null` and the library silently accepts them as disabled reject-on-clear behavior, despite the option being a boolean contract. This makes runtime behavior depend on truthiness rather than type.
findings.evidence: index.js:12-14 only validates truthy values; readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 declare the option type as boolean; index.test-d.ts only catches the TypeScript string case and no runtime test covers falsy non-booleans.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module: `pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0})`, `''`, and `null` all constructed successfully instead of throwing `Expected rejectOnClear to be a boolean`.
